title: Build a Blog: Posts, Categories, Tags and a Menu

chapters.title: Build a Blog: Posts, Categories, Tags and a Menu
chapters.subtitle: Posts, categories, tags and a menu with The Blog Theme

steps.text: A blog is a list of posts that visitors can browse by category and by tag, with a menu to find their way around. In this video, you build one with The Blog Theme: a category, a post with tags, and a menu item.

chapters.title: How a blog fits together
chapters.subtitle: The Blog recipe and its parts

steps.text: The Blog recipe sets up a site for a blog. It creates the content types, a blog with a first post, the Categories and Tags taxonomies, and a Main Menu, and it activates The Blog Theme.
The Blog is a list. It contains Blog Posts, shown with the most recent first, and it is the home page of the site. Each post has a title, a subtitle, a banner image, and a body.

A taxonomy is a set of terms that you attach to content. A post can have one category, chosen from the Categories taxonomy, and any number of tags, taken from the Tags taxonomy. Both appear as badges on the post.
You add a category, write a post, see where its tags are kept, and add an item to the Main Menu. Along the way, you meet the permalink: the address that each page gets on the site.
This is the home page of the site, and it is the Blog. The banner shows its title and description. Below come the posts, each with a subtitle, an author, a date, and badges for its category and tags.
At the top right, the Main Menu holds two items, Home and About. The name of the site stands on the left.
Opening a post shows its banner image, title, subtitle, and body. Under the text, the category and each tag link to a page that lists the posts they share.
In the admin, the Blog item of the menu opens the Blog and the list of its posts. Create Blog Post adds a post to this blog, and Edit Blog changes the blog itself.
Edit Blog shows how the blog is addressed. Its Permalink is blog, and a note says that this content item is the current homepage, which is why the site opens on the blog.
The footer at the bottom of every page is a widget. In the admin, Design, Widgets opens Widgets and Layers: the Footer zone holds it, and its badge names the layer, Always.

chapters.title: Add a category
chapters.subtitle: A term of the Categories taxonomy

steps.text: Categories are the terms of a taxonomy. In the admin menu, Content, Taxonomy lists the taxonomies of the site. Let's edit Categories.
The editor lists the terms of the taxonomy: here, Travel. Add Category creates a category at the top level, and the Add button of a term creates a subcategory inside it.
Let's add Photography. The title is the name of the category. The Permalink is the end of the address of its page, so let's type photography.
The Icon field is required. It opens a picker, and the icon appears next to the name of the category on the site. On this page, Publish adds the category to a draft of the taxonomy.
A draft is not visible to visitors, so the taxonomy needs a Publish of its own. After that, the category is part of the site.

chapters.title: Write a post
chapters.subtitle: Title, image, body, category and tags

steps.text: From the Blog, Create Blog Post opens the editor of a post. Let's type the title and leave the Permalink empty: the address is built from the blog and the title, unless you type your own.
The body is written in Markdown, which is plain text with simple marks for formatting. Let's write a sentence.
The Subtitle shows under the title. For the Banner Image, Add media opens the media library: select an image and click OK.
Tags searches as you type. Type to search the tags that exist, and select one. Let's select Exploration.
When no tag matches, the field offers Press enter to create a tag. Let's type Lisbon and press Enter: the tag is created in the Tags taxonomy and selected for this post.
Category lists the categories of the taxonomy, and a post can have one. Only a category without subcategories can be chosen. Let's choose Photography.
Publish saves the post and returns to the Blog, with a message that the post is published. The list shows the post at the top. Save Draft would keep it hidden from visitors.
On the site, the post comes first on the home page, with badges for Photography, Exploration and Lisbon. Opening it shows the banner, the subtitle and the text.
Each tag links to a page of its own. Lisbon lists the posts that have this tag, which is the post we wrote.
Tags are the terms of the Tags taxonomy. In the admin, Content, Taxonomy lists it, and its editor holds Lisbon next to the other tags. A tag created from a post is published at once.
Add Tag creates a tag here as well. The tag field of a post creates tags only for users who have the Manage taxonomies permission.
Main Menu in the admin menu opens the editor of the menu. Its Alias field holds main-menu: The Blog Theme finds the menu by this alias, so keep it unchanged.
Below, the editor lists the items, Home and About. Add Menu Item opens a dialog named Available Menu Items.
It offers three types. A Link Menu Item links to a custom address, a Content Menu Item links to a content item, and an Html Menu Item uses HTML for the text of the link.
Let's add a Link Menu Item. The Name is the text visitors see, and the Url is where it leads. Photography leads to the page of the category.
Publish adds the item to a draft of the menu, and the editor lists it after Home and About. As with a taxonomy, visitors see the change only after the menu itself is published.
Let's publish the menu. Dragging an item changes its order, and the Add button of an item adds an item inside it, which the theme shows as a drop-down.
On the site, the menu shows Photography after About. Clicking it opens the page of the category, which lists the post we wrote.

steps.text: A blog needs a few parts: a Blog with its posts, categories and tags to organize them, a Main Menu to move around, and a permalink for every page. Thanks for watching.
